lesson.title: sing/sang/sung Mirrors
lesson.subtitle: Map ten English irregulars onto their German ablauf pairs

hook.title: Ten Mirrors on the Wall
hook.content: You have heard the melody in pairs. Today is the gallery: ten English irregular verbs hung beside their German twins, class by class. sing ↔ singen. drink ↔ trinken. find ↔ finden. give ↔ geben. speak ↔ sprechen. come ↔ kommen. schreiben's English kin is the scribe family (scribe, describe, script). drive ↔ treiben. fare ↔ fahren. sleep ↔ schlafen (sleep/slept ↔ schlafen/schlief — the vowels drift but the CLASS is identical). Stand in front of each pair and the recognition does the memorizing: the melody is not similar. It is the same.

footnotes.title: The Class Map
footnotes.content: Proto-Germanic sorted strong verbs into seven classes by their vowel melody. English forgot the numbering; German grammars keep it. You only need the echoes: i-a-u (sing), ei-ie-ie (schreiben), a-u (fahren). When an English verb and a German verb share a class, they share a history.

pattern.title: The Gallery Walk
pattern.content: Walk it: singen, sang, gesungen ↔ sing, sang, sung. trinken, trank, getrunken ↔ drink, drank, drunk. finden, fand, gefunden ↔ find, found. geben, gab, gegeben ↔ give, gave, given. kommen, kam, gekommen ↔ come, came (the vowel wandered, the class held). schreiben, schrieb, geschrieben ↔ describe, described (scribe family). fahren, fuhr, gefahren ↔ fare, fared. schlafen, schlief, geschlafen ↔ sleep, slept. Ten frames, one artist — the melody is the same artist in every language.
pattern.linguist_note: schlafen/schlief ↔ sleep/slept is the cleanest proof that classes are inherited, not coincidence: the consonants match, the vowels follow the same class drift, and neither language arranged this on purpose.

exercises.prompt: Gallery wall one — match the melodies:
exercises.target_answer: sprechen / sprach / gesprochen, kommen / kam / gekommen, schreiben / schrieb / geschrieben, schlafen / schlief
exercises.meaning: the speak, come, scribe, sleep melodies
exercises.explanation: Same classes, same vowels, same history — the gallery wall of shared inheritance.

exercises.prompt: Which English verb family is the true relative of 'schreiben / schrieb / geschrieben'?
exercises.meaning: schreiben belongs to the scribe family, not write's family
exercises.explanation: schreiben is Latin scribere Germanicized — its English relatives are scribe, describe, script. Write/wrote is an unrelated native word.
kommen, kam, gekommen ↔ come, came, come — the vowel moved in both languages, the class never moved.

exercises.prompt: Answer the question in the conversational past:
cues: Place gestern in the middle and geschlafen at the end of the bracket.
exercises.explanation: haben sits in position two while the strong participle geschlafen closes the sentence bracket.
Strong participle gesprochen closes the bracket — sprechen, sprach, gesprochen ↔ speak, spoke, spoken.

summary.outcome: Map ten English irregulars to their German ablauf twins by class.
summary.takeaway: The irregular verbs are not lists — they are ten mirrors of one Germanic melody system.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Ablaut Families I — the e→i and a→o classes drilled with geben, sprechen and fahren.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "We sing here today"
twist.explanation: Building "Wir singen heute hier" from the lesson's core pattern locks in sing/sang/sung Mirrors.

singen.etymology_derivation: Initial S voiced to [z] before vowels.

trinken.context_translation: I drink a glass of water.

finden.context_translation: I cannot find it / I find it not.
finden.etymology_derivation: Stem find + infinitive -en (German keeps pure short [ɪ] vowel).

geben.context_translation: There is a problem (literally: it gives a problem).
geben.etymology_derivation: v → b. In impersonal form "es gibt", expresses existence.

nehmen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *nemaną — the twin of archaic English nim 'to take', surviving in nimble ('quick to grasp'); English take is a Norse import. [wiktionary]

fahren.context_translation: I am going / driving to Berlin.
fahren.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *faraną — the twin of English fare (farewell, bus fare, 'how did you fare?'). [wiktionary]

schreiben.etymology_derivation: A Latin loan (scribere) that both languages Germanicized — English kept it in scribe, script, describe. Strong verb: schrieb, geschrieben. [wiktionary]

schlafen.etymology_derivation: p → f with sl- → schl- cluster.

natürlich.context_translation: Of course I will gladly help you.
natürlich.etymology_derivation: Natur + -lich — Wiktionary cross-references English naturally; the same classical loan line. [wiktionary]

gefährlich.etymology_derivation: Gefahr (danger) plus -lich; Gefahr goes back to Proto-Germanic *fērō, which is also the ancestor of English fear — German kept the old meaning danger, while English drifted to the feeling that danger produces. [wiktionary]

rucksack.context_phrase: Im Rucksack sind Wasser und Brot.
rucksack.context_translation: In the backpack there are water and bread.
rucksack.etymology_derivation: Rücken (back) + Sack (sack); English borrowed rucksack directly from German, and Sack itself is the same word in both languages. [wiktionary]

eigentlich.etymology_derivation: Eigen (twin of English own) plus -lich (twin of -ly) — originally ownly, in truth, now mainly actually; inherited from Middle High German eigenliche. [wiktionary]

verwandte.etymology_derivation: Substantivized from the adjective verwandt, the past participle of verwenden; the etymology section on the page is empty, so the traditional link to English wend via wenden, to turn, is not documented there. [wiktionary] [UNVERIFIED - check]

hauptbahnhof.context_translation: We are meeting at the main station.
hauptbahnhof.etymology_derivation: Haupt + Bahnhof — the head-station; Haupt traces to the Proto-Indo-European *kap- head root (Latin caput, English head). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
